405904.title: Lost Things Wait to Be Found
405904.overview:
A group show on how memory is reproduced through records and images. Records today are easier than ever to make and store, yet much of what we save is never reopened – not lost, but out of place. The exhibition likens these records to lost property: like a lost item, a record only becomes memory again when someone looks at it.

Kim So-ra traces letters from Korean nurses sent to West Germany in the 1970s and records of women factory workers. Nozomi Suzuki prints, onto old objects coated with photo emulsion, the views they once faced. Lea Belooussovitch redraws news photos of disasters in coloured pencil on felt. Choi In-young, raised in a Taean fishing village, works with nets, family videotapes and discarded objects.

405589.title: Suspicious Surfaces
405589.overview:
Three glass artists – Shin Jisoo, Jang Chaelin and Choi Sangjun – start from the moment our familiar judgements about appearances stop holding true.

Shin finds the potential for new life in mould, usually read as decay. Jang creates fixed glass forms whose colours and images shift with the light and the viewer's position. Choi's Beardman draws the eye with vivid colours and patterns, yet its elaborate exterior is also a means of concealment and self-protection.

Rather than asking visitors to find hidden answers, the show invites them to look a little longer, change position and reconsider their first impressions.

407639.title: Park Gyeol: Where the Souls Linger
407639.overview:
We often compare life to a film. Not every scene goes as planned, and sometimes we need to call "OK, cut" on an imperfect take and pause – not to give up, but to move on to the next scene.

Park Gyeol's exhibition is about the spaces between life's scenes, where souls linger for a while for their own sake. Its journey runs from light seeping in and being absorbed to endurance and flight: souls sit watching the sunset, looking back on the light left in them. The love, hope and comfort we receive do not vanish; they seep in and become light. Rather than urging visitors onward, the show suggests they stay a moment for themselves.

405479.title: Lee Chang-nam: Where Cool Meets Warm – Studio Curtain
405479.overview:
Paintings by Lee Chang-nam, whose canvases are built from thousands of precisely judged colours and touches – in a still life of pink roses in a glass vase, every brushstroke plays its part in rendering glass, water, petals and shadow.

Lee repeatedly paints his own studio, the space he knows through his own perception, and the views from it: villas below the Geumho-dong hill, new apartment towers, the Han River and the Gangnam skyline, recording a decade of change. The highlight of this show is a series of paintings featuring a floral-patterned curtain at the studio window, marking the threshold between his interior world and the bright city outside. (Based on an essay by Jeong Shin-young, Seoul Women's University.)

405588.title: Kim Han-na: Paper, Pencil, Eraser, Book
405588.overview:
The title names four objects always on the artist's desk – and the act of drawing they make possible: waiting before a blank sheet, drawing a line, erasing and drawing again.

Kim Han-na is known for a world built around an imaginary rabbit, spanning painting, drawing, sculpture, animation and picture books. Here she returns to the hand, with oil paintings such as Rabbit Pencil, Pencil Smell Connoisseur and Let's Draw a Road, and drawings combining coloured pencil, oil pastel and acrylic on paper. Faint traces of erasure and layered paint show the time each work has passed through. The catalogue includes a preface written as a children's poem by the poet Oh Eun.

407030.title: Park YongHo: Continuum
407030.overview:
Recent works by Park YongHo, the fruit of three years of patient labour. The work grows from a childhood question – "What lies beyond?" – that led him to the cosmos and quantum mechanics, and to the realisation that the world we perceive is only a fragment shaped by reality and perception together.

Park cuts, shapes and paints metal plates, then interlaces the squared and rounded pieces on the front and back of grid frames. As they conceal and reveal one another, they create layered depth and graded shadows that change as visitors move. The title suggests that the relationships of the world never reach a final state, each part joining an ever larger whole.

406391.title: Woo Byung-chul Solo Exhibition
406391.overview:
Woo Byung-chul paints the everyday city – dense buildings, traffic-filled roads, hurrying crowds – through a meticulous, persistent accumulation of lines. From a distance each work reads as a complete cityscape; up close, countless lines, dots and touches of colour reveal the time and patience behind it.

Repeated lines meet to form planes and spaces, finding unexpected order and beauty in the tangle of the city, while finely drawn structures and selective accents of colour give the scenes their energy. The exhibition invites visitors to pause, look again at familiar places and rediscover the beauty hidden in daily life.

407031.title: The Theoretical Practice of Architect Jung Jin-kook
407031.overview:
A survey of Jung Jin-kook's work as an architect, architectural historian and educator. It brings together four models of Le Corbusier houses (Maison La Roche-Jeanneret, Villa Stein-de Monzie, Villa Besnus and Villa Savoye) that he made in Paris in 1991 while preparing his doctorate, ten models of his own buildings designed on the basis of his theories, and fourteen panels. Two of his books are also introduced: a study of Le Corbusier's ten theories, distilled from 30 years of research, and Generalisation, on inductive method in architectural form.

On Sat 7 November at 4pm Jung gives a talk on Le Corbusier in the B1 seminar room.

407032.title: Between Forms
407032.overview:
Atelier Aki's final curated show of 2026 brings together three millennial artists working in sculpture, Korean ink painting and oil painting. Greem Jeong extends a single continuous line into sculptural furniture and lighting, as in her Mono Series and Knot Chair. Jin Jihyun layers ink and colour on hanji paper to paint birds, moons and flowers in which everyday reality meets inner "ghosts" of memory and emotion. Yuseong Choe lets bodily movement and the behaviour of oil paint guide her compositions, presenting new works for the first time.

The "between" of the title refers to the relationships that arise as forms are made and interpreted.

407638.title: Park Ji-hoon: Times of Conjecture
407638.overview:
Park Ji-hoon's solo show is about the possibility of communication between viewer and artist. At large exhibitions such as biennales, visitors tend to reach first for guidebooks and wall texts, and end up "reading" works rather than looking at them.

To question this habit, the exhibition deliberately keeps text and information to a minimum, and some works are simply titled Untitled. The resulting unease is part of the intended experience: instead of supplying a fixed interpretation, the show leaves room for visitors to meet the works through their own senses and experience.

402249.title: Saturday Gugak Masterpieces
402249.overview: The National Gugak Center's signature weekend show, presenting traditional Korean music in depth and variety in an ideal setting. Every Saturday the Woomyeondang stage is filled with song, music and dance full of Korean spirit and joy, including UNESCO-listed intangible cultural heritage, performed by some of the country's finest musicians – an essential introduction to Korean traditional performing arts for Koreans and international visitors alike.

402251.title: Saturday Gugak Fairy Tales
402251.overview: Every Saturday afternoon, this family show tells engaging stories with traditional Korean music pitched at children's level. It takes place in Pungnyu Sarangbang, a hanok-style hall with natural, unamplified acoustics, and is designed to nurture a feel for gugak. Open to everyone aged 12 months and over.

403447.title: Han Young-jun: Gaein (Open Person)
403447.overview:
A solo show by Han Young-jun that sets theory aside to follow the most natural path of the brush. The title, Gaein, means a person who opens up a closed frame and expands, and also the process of an individual gently opening the time and emotions of their life onto canvas.

His subjects follow his life: early colour experiments, figures from the pandemic years, his mother's illness and his time caring for her, plein-air painting born of longing for the outdoors while in hospital, and his new family. The works are shown side by side without being tied to one style or series. Open 10:30–18:00, closed Sundays; opening reception 11 November, 5pm.
